īśvarapraṇidhāna
(‘devotion to ईश्वर or God’)
------------------------------------------
This is a special word used in the Yogasūtras (1.23) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.).
After describing a few methods for suppressing the modifications of मिन्द्, पतञ्जलि, apparently recognising the desire of a sādhaka for an easy method, is giving it in this sūtra.
Īśvara is God and praṇidhāna is devotion. This devotion must express itself in the form of dedicating the fruits of all our actions unto him. When he is pleased, he may give even समाधि, what to speak of lesser states of योग.

Īśvaragītā
(‘[the teaching] sung by ईश्वर or शिव’)
------------------------------------------
The Bhagavadgītā has, in course of time, given rise to a number of similar religio-philosophical treatises, either as a part of the epics or of the various पुराणस्. One such famous work, the Īśvaragītā, occurs in the uttarabhāga or the second part of the Kūrmapurāṇa. The first eleven chapters of this purāṇa containing 496 ślokas in all, comprise the Īśvaragītā. It is called Īśvaragītā because ईश्वर or शिव is the teacher, answering the questions put to him by the various sages like Sanatkumāra, Sanandana, सनक, Aṅgirā, भृगु, कपिल, वसिष्ठ and others who had assembled at the बदरिकाश्रम.
A brief synopsis of the contents may now be given here:
Description of ईश्वर or आत्मन् as the non-dual Reality, as Sat-cit-आनन्द.
Evolution of this world from प्रधान or प्रकृति, the details being similar to the ones given in Sāṅkhya philosophy.
The glory of शिव in Vedāntic terms emphasising the path of भक्ति or devotion.
Cosmic dance of शिव and his eulogy by the sages.
Description of शिव’s vibhūtis or various manifestations.
Realising शिव in one’s heart as the means of लिबेरतिओन्.
Identity of ईश्वर or शिव and परब्रह्मन्, the Absolute.
The path of लिबेरतिओन् wherein funda-mental ethical virtues like अहिṁसा (nonviolence), सत्य (truth), ब्रह्मचर्य (continence) and others have an important place. So also स्वाध्याय (study of scriptures), तपस् (austerity), प्राणायाम (control of breath) and the eight steps of योग.
The work closes with the narration of the line of teachers as also the phalaśruti (eulogy of this spiritual wisdom).
Vijñānabhikṣu (16th cent. A. D.) wrote a commentary called Īśvaragītābhāṣya which is fairly exhaustive.

He was born in A.

in a small village of Midnapur district (in West Bengal) and came to Calcutta (now Kolkata) at the age of nine for higher एदुचतिओन्. Pursuing his एदुचतिओन् in the midst of many difficulties, he got his title ‘Vidyāsāgara’ in his nineteenth year from the Sanskrit Mahāpāṭhaśālā where he studied.
He worked as a Sanskrit teacher in the Fort William College. When he was offered the post of the professor of व्याकरण (grammar of Sanskrit) in the Mahāpāṭhaśālā where he had studied, he felt that Tārānātha Tarkavācaspati (A.

-1885) was a better candidate and prevailed upon him to accept it, after walking a distance of 161 kms. (100 miles) to his place of residence!
He later on became the principal of the Fort William College wherein he successfully introduced some badly needed reforms. This enabled the members of the non-ब्राह्मण classes also to learn Sanskrit.
In course of time he resigned his job and started his own educational institution.
Throughout his life, he struggled with the orthodox and begoted sections of the Hindu society to introduce some urgent social reforms like the remarriage of child-widows. He was one of the important leaders of this movement. The spirit of this movement spread to several other parts of India also.
He fought against the social system of पोल्य्गम्य् which was rampant in the Hindu society also.
His literary works in Bengali are: Betālapañcaviṁśati, Śākuntalā and Sītāparityāga. The last work has been considered as his best.
He breathed his last in July 1891.

The Sāṅkhyadarśana or the Sāṅkhya philosophy, is nearest to Vedānta (since it tries to get support from the उपनिषद्स्) but has also deviated from it. It is because of this that बादरायण व्यास, the author of the Brahmasūtras, has taken it up first for refutation.
Though it is difficult to say when exactly this deviation and separation took place, the Sāṅkhyakārikā of ईश्वरकृष्ण is certainly the earliest of the cardinal works of this system.
Practically next to nothing is known of this ईश्वरकृष्ण. He might have lived some time during the period A.

-450. He was a ब्राह्मण of the कौशिक गोत्र (lineage of the sage कौशिक) and was a monk. He was probably a follower of वार्षगण्य, a teacher of Sāṅkhya mentioned in the Mahābhārata (306.57).

Īśvara
(‘one who rules,’ ‘the Lord’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘Īśvara’ has been used in the Hindu scriptural works both in a general sense and in a more particular sense. In a general sense it means ‘God’. In the restricted sense it stands for शिव, the last deity of the Hindu Trinity.
See GOD and ŚIVA for details.
In Advaita Vedānta, the word is used to indicate ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, after becoming conscious of his power of māyā and reflecting on the process of च्रेअतिओन्. Sometimes other names such as अव्यक्त (the Unmanifested), Jagatkāraṇa (the cause of the world), अन्तर्यामिन् (the inner controller) are also used.
